finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id calls async authorize() without await, so the grant check never gates db.reports.remove. Any caller, including one with no session, can delete any report.
finding.source: Path param :id (server.js:18); req.user taken from req.session.user (server.js:5)

trace.note: report loaded by id with no owner or tenant scope
authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) called without await; returns a Promise that is ignored
authorize is async; a denied grant or undefined user throws inside it, producing an unhandled rejection rather than gating the handler
remove executes regardless of the authorization outcome

finding.guards_checked: Only guard on path is authorize() at line 20, which is not awaited so cannot gate line 21. grants.includes logic (server.js:10-15) is correct but has no effect here. PUT route (server.js:27) awaits the same helper, showing DELETE is inconsistent. No session-presence check exists in this file.

verdict.guard_found: The only candidate guard is authorize(req.user, "delete", report) at server.js:20. It is an async function (server.js:9) that signals denial by throwing (server.js:14), and it is called as a bare statement without await, so its Promise is discarded and its rejection never reaches the handler. The middleware at server.js:4-7 only copies req.session.user and enforces no authentication. The grants check at server.js:10-11 is correct but cannot gate anything. Line 21 (db.reports.remove) runs unconditionally.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls the async authorize() without await, so its denial throw at server.js:14 becomes an unhandled rejection and server.js:21 deletes the report regardless of the grant result. Any authenticated user who can reach this route (as in the PUT route at server.js:27, which awaits the same helper) can delete reports they have no grant for. The "no session at all" variant is only plausible if session middleware (not in this file) sets req.session to an object with no user, because server.js:5 would throw before the handler if req.session were undefined; the core finding holds for any authenticated low-privilege user.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire client request body to db.reports.update, so any client-supplied field, including server-managed columns, can be written by a caller who has write permission.
finding.source: JSON request body parsed by express.json() (server.js:3)

trace.note: express.json() parses full body with no field filtering
entire req.body passed to update with no allow-list

finding.guards_checked: write-permission check at server.js:27 is awaited and correct but is object-level only; no field allow-list or schema filter exists in this file. id comes from the URL, so a body id alone does not retarget the row unless the db layer uses body.id (unverified).

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)`, which throws a 403 at server.js:14 when the grant is missing. This is an effective object-level check, so the write is reachable only by a session user holding a write grant on that report. No field allow-list or schema filter exists in server.js. The directory holds only server.js, so the db layer (`db.reports.update`) is not visible.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: express.json() at server.js:3 parses the body, and server.js:28 passes all of req.body to db.reports.update after the awaited write check at server.js:27 succeeds. The mass-assignment pattern is real, but whether it is a vulnerability depends on which columns db.reports.update writes and whether any are server-managed (e.g. owner or id). Neither the schema nor the update implementation is in the directory, so the "server-managed columns" impact cannot be confirmed.
